analysis.summary:
This sixty-eight-year-old male presents a classic picture of chronic Damp-Heat dermatitis superimposed upon a foundation of constitutional Spleen Qi deficiency. The twenty-year history of scaly red rash with severe itching, now acutely worse, combined with the constellation of digestive complaints—poor appetite, heavy sensation, sticky stools with incomplete evacuation—points unmistakably to Spleen dysfunction as the root pathology. The sticky mouth, yellow greasy tongue coating, slippery-rapid pulse, and yellowish exudate with crusting on skin all confirm the concurrent Damp-Heat pattern.

The tongue findings are diagnostic: a red base indicates underlying Heat and Yin insufficiency from chronic disease; the yellow greasy coating is pathognomonic for Damp-Heat. The slippery-rapid pulse confirms Damp-Heat in excess, while the underlying Qi-deficient constitution (evident from fatigue, poor appetite, and loose stools) indicates that the Spleen is too weak to clear the Damp-Heat efficiently. This is a critical diagnostic point: treating only the Heat without supporting the Spleen would worsen the foundation and likely cause rebound flaring.

The acute exacerbation in the last week suggests a precipitating factor—possibly dietary indiscretion (greasy or sweet foods that further overwhelm Spleen function), emotional stress (causing Liver Qi stagnation that impairs Spleen transport), or seasonal climatic shift. The sleep disturbance from itching adds a secondary Heart-Spleen component: the itching agitates the Spirit, and the underlying Qi deficiency weakens the Heart's ability to anchor the Spirit at night.

From an Eight Principles perspective: the presentation is clearly Interior (chronic systemic involvement), Heat (red rash, rapid pulse, yellow exudate, bitter taste of Damp-Heat), Mixed Deficiency-Excess (Excess Damp-Heat manifestation with underlying Deficient Spleen Qi), and overall leaning toward Yang-type presentation with Yin insufficiency from long-standing disease. The therapeutic challenge is to clear the acute Heat-Damp without further depleting Spleen Qi—a careful balancing act that requires cautious use of cold clearing herbs paired with Spleen-fortifying support.

key_findings.from_inquiry: Twenty-year history of recurrent scaly red rash with severe itching, acutely worse in the last week; sticky mouth sensation suggesting Damp-Heat in Spleen; poor appetite and fatigue indicating Spleen Qi deficiency; heavy body sensation typical of Dampness; sticky stools with incomplete evacuation showing Spleen's failure to transform; yellowish exudate and crusting indicating Heat toxicity; sleep disturbance from itching revealing Spirit agitation secondary to Damp-Heat
key_findings.from_visual: Tongue red (Heat, Yin insufficiency) with yellow greasy coating (Damp-Heat, classic for Spleen pattern); visible scaly red rash with yellowish exudate and crusting (Heat toxicity seeking outlet through skin; Wei Qi insufficiency); overall appearance suggests fatigue and constitutional weakness
key_findings.from_pulse: Slippery pulse (hua mai—indicates Dampness, fluids in excess) and rapid pulse (shu mai—indicates Heat) together form the textbook 'slippery-rapid' pattern of Damp-Heat; absence of other pulse qualities (thin, weak) suggests that while Qi is deficient, it has not yet collapsed into true vacuity pulse
key_findings.from_other: The twenty-year duration indicates this is a chronic constitutional pattern, not acute exogenous disease; the combination of digestive weakness with skin manifestation confirms Spleen as the organ system in imbalance; no fever, chills, or systemic toxicity signs suggest this is chronic Damp-Heat rather than acute infection, ruling out need for aggressive clearing

analysis.pattern_rationale: The diagnosis of Damp-Heat with underlying Spleen Qi Deficiency is supported by six converging lines of evidence: (1) Tongue findings—red base with yellow greasy coat is virtually pathognomonic for Damp-Heat pattern affecting the Spleen system; (2) Pulse—the combination of slippery (Damp) and rapid (Heat) is the classic pulse for Damp-Heat, precisely matching the pathology; (3) Digestive signs—poor appetite, fatigue, loose stool, sticky stool with incomplete evacuation, heavy sensation all point directly to Spleen Qi weakness unable to transform food and fluids; (4) Skin manifestation—the twenty-year chronic rash with yellowish weeping suggests Heat-Damp seeking outlet through skin when Wei Qi becomes insufficient; the recent acute flare indicates an exogenous or dietary trigger has overwhelmed the weakened system; (5) Sticky mouth—a specific indicator of Damp-Heat affecting the Spleen's fluid-transformation function; (6) Sleep disturbance from itching—indicates that Damp-Heat agitation (Excess pathogen) is superimposed on Qi deficiency (insufficient resources to resist pathogen). This is not a simple Excess Damp-Heat pattern (which would show strong appetite and normal energy) nor a simple Qi-deficiency pattern (which would lack the yellow coating and rapid pulse). The dual nature requires a dual treatment approach addressing both the Excess pathogen and the Deficient foundation.

treatment.therapeutic_principle: Clear and drain Damp-Heat from the Lower Burner while fortifying Spleen Qi; resolve toxicity from the skin while supporting Wei Qi recovery; in the acute phase, prioritize Heat-Damp clearing with gentle Spleen support; in the maintenance phase, transition to constitutional Spleen Qi fortification with residual Damp clearing to prevent recurrence
treatment.treatment_method: In acute phase (one to two weeks): Use formulas that combine bitter cold Damp-Heat clearing herbs (Cang Zhu, Huang Bai) with warm Spleen-fortifying herbs (Bai Zhu, Fu Ling, Gan Cao) to avoid the iatrogenic complication of injuring Spleen Yang through excessive cold. Incorporate blood-invigorating herbs (Chi Shao) to address the skin redness and reduce inflammation without stagnating qi. In maintenance phase (weeks two through eight): Transition to Si Jun Zi Tang (Four Gentlemen Decoction) as the base formula to rebuild Spleen Qi, adding Job's Tears and red dates to gently clear residual Damp and nourish blood for skin healing. Implement dietary therapy using warm, easily-digestible foods that support Spleen transformation. Add acupoint self-massage targeting Spleen and Qi-supplementing points. Modify lifestyle to reduce Spleen-damaging factors (cold foods, greasy foods, worry) and support Spleen Yang (warmth, consistent meal timing, gentle movement). Expect progressive improvement over three to six months as constitution strengthens.

beneficial: Job's Tears (Yi Mi / Coix lacryma-jobi) — sweet, bland, and slightly cool; directly strengthens Spleen's transformation and transportation function without being excessively cold that would damage Spleen Yang; simultaneously drains accumulated Dampness through gradual gentle action; reduces skin itching and weeping through its specific affinity for this pattern

Chinese Winter Melon (Dong Gua / Benincasa hispida) — sweet and cool; effectively drains Damp-Heat through the urine without injuring Spleen; clears excess Heat from the Large Intestine reducing intestinal Damp-Heat manifestation; very light and easy to digest even for weak Spleen

Mung Bean (Lv Dou) — sweet and cool; one of the premier Heat-toxicity resolvers for skin conditions; clears Heat without the harsh cold that would create counterinjury to Spleen; helps resolve weeping and crusting through topical and internal Heat reduction; safe for long-term use

Pearl Barley / Hulled Barley (Da Mai) — sweet, cool, neutral; strengthens Spleen's transformation and transportation similar to Job's Tears but with slightly easier digestibility for very weak Spleen; gently clears residual Heat without harsh cold properties; combines Dampness-elimination with subtle Qi-support

Fresh Water Fish or Carp (Qingdan Bai Rou Yu) — bland, sweet, and warm-neutral; provides high-quality protein that supports Spleen's Qi-building without the inflammatory heat-generating properties of beef or mutton; assists Spleen in nutrient extraction and Qi generation; easier to digest than heavier meats
recipes: Job's Tears and Red Date Congee (Yi Mi Hong Zao Zhou): Combine 30g Job's Tears, 3 whole red dates, 30g white rice, and 800ml water. Bring to boil, then simmer for 45 minutes until all grains are soft and congee reaches desired consistency. Consume warm as breakfast or light dinner, one bowl daily. Purpose: Fortifies Spleen Qi while gradually clearing Dampness; red dates supplement Qi and blood essential for skin repair and healing; warm temperature supports Spleen Yang function; mild flavor prevents further Spleen stagnation from heavy seasoning

Winter Melon and Barley Pork Rib Soup (Dong Gua Da Mai Zhu Pai Tang): Blanch 100g pork ribs briefly; combine with 300g winter melon (cut into chunks), 30g Job's Tears, 20g pearl barley, 3 slices fresh ginger, and 1500ml water. Simmer for 90 minutes until broth is clear and pork is tender. Add salt to taste at end. Consume broth and solids, one bowl daily. Purpose: Drains Damp-Heat through winter melon's diuretic action; fortifies Spleen and aids digestion through grain combination; ginger warms digestion without excess heat; pork provides gentle Qi-supplementation; complete meal in one bowl addressing both acute clearing and constitutional support

foods_to_avoid: Greasy and fried foods (You Zha, Fei Rou) — directly exacerbate Spleen's already-impaired ability to digest and transform fats; increase Dampness generation; fatty saturation worsens the weeping and exudate from skin by providing pathogenic fluid substrate; even one meal of greasy food can trigger multi-day flaring

Spicy and hot foods (Xin La, Shao Kao) — further heat the already-inflamed skin lesions; trigger Liver Fire which impairs Spleen's transport function; irritate the intestinal lining exacerbating sticky stool pattern; create additional inflammation that manifests as rash intensification

Cold and raw foods (Bing Leng, Sheng Leng) — directly damage Spleen Yang which is already insufficient to generate transformation heat; impair digestive fire leading to further Damp accumulation; ice water and refrigerated foods are particularly problematic; ice suppresses acute flare temporarily but fundamentally worsens the underlying Qi deficiency making long-term condition worse
lifestyle: Maintain warmth while avoiding excess external heat — avoid direct air conditioning on skin and prolonged sun exposure as both aggravate chronic dermatitis; dress in breathable cotton allowing gentle ventilation without cold exposure; maintain room temperature at 22-24 degrees Celsius (comfortable range without requiring heavy heating); warm environment supports Spleen Yang function whereas cold impairs it

Regulate meal timing and portion sizes for Spleen support — consume warm meals at consistent times each day (breakfast 07:30, lunch 12:00, dinner 18:30) to allow Spleen to prepare and function optimally; eat only until 70 percent full to avoid overwhelming weak digestive capacity; avoid eating after 20:00 as late eating stagnates Spleen leading to next-day fatigue and poor appetite

Implement gentle physical activity in early morning hours — perform twenty to thirty minutes of slow walking at 06:30-07:30 AM in park or nature setting; avoid vigorous exercise which depletes Qi in acute inflammatory phase; gentle movement promotes Qi circulation and supports Spleen transport without exhaustion; walking on flat terrain better than stairs or hills for this constitution

Manage emotional stress and establish consistent sleep hygiene — avoid excessive worry and rumination which directly damage Spleen function (worry is the Spleen's emotional association); maintain consistent sleep schedule from 23:00 to 07:00 allowing Spleen-Stomach to undergo rest and Qi restoration; practice five-minute guided relaxation meditation immediately before bed to calm the Spirit agitation from itching; consider writing down worries before bed to externalize them and prevent rumination
acupoints: Zusanli (ST36 足三里) — Located 3 cun (approximately 10 cm using patient's proportional cun) directly below Dubi (ST35, the depression below the kneecap on the outer leg), positioned one finger-breadth lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bone ridge on the front and outside of the lower leg). Technique: Apply firm sustained pressure using thumb or knuckle for two to three minutes with small circular massage motions or static pressure; repeat one to two times daily (morning and evening). Purpose: Master point for Spleen and Stomach that fortifies Qi and supports gastrointestinal function even in advanced age; simultaneously boosts Wei (defensive) Qi to strengthen the skin barrier against pathogenic Damp-Heat; considered the primary point for constitutional strengthening and longevity support in traditional Chinese medicine

Sanyinjiao (SP6 三阴交) — Located 3 cun directly above the medial malleolus (inner ankle bone), positioned on the medial (inner) border of the tibia (shin bone). Technique: Apply sustained pressure or gentle rubbing motion using thumb for two to three minutes, performing this massage morning and evening, three to six days per week. Purpose: Critical point that regulates Spleen's blood-nourishing and fluid-transformation functions; directly addresses the Damp-Heat pattern in the lower burner; improves digestive transformation and food intake; improves sleep quality and reduces nocturnal itching through Shen-calming action; safe point for older patients with no contraindications

Geshu (BL17 膈俞) — Located on the back in the paraspinal groove (the channel running vertical beside the spine), positioned at the level of the 7th intercostal space, which corresponds approximately to the level of the inferior (lower) angle of the scapula (shoulder blade). Technique: Apply light to medium pressure using thumb or knuckle with gentle pinching or circular massage for one to two minutes, performed daily in morning or evening; may require partner assistance to reach. Purpose: Governs blood and supports nutritive Qi; essential point for addressing chronic skin conditions that require blood-nourishing to repair damaged dermis; aids in coordination of Lung-Spleen in the generation and distribution of Qi and blood; supports overall Qi supplementation in older patients with deficiency patterns

Xuehai (SP10 血海) — Located on the medial (inner) thigh, 2 cun above the medial end of the knee crease (where the knee bends), positioned on the vastus medialis muscle (inner thigh muscle above knee). Technique: Apply firm rubbing or acupressure using thumb for two minutes, one to two times daily (morning and evening); this point is accessible and effective for self-care. Purpose: Primary point for regulating blood circulation and resolving chronic itching skin diseases through blood-level intervention; directly addresses the manifestation of rash and itching through local and systemic blood activation; strengthens Spleen's blood-controlling and nourishing functions; prevents blood stagnation which would perpetuate skin inflammation
exercise: Tai Chi (Tai Ji Quan) or Qi Gong, specifically the Eight Pieces of Silk (Ba Duan Jin 八段锦) — Perform twenty to thirty minutes daily, five to six days per week, preferably in early morning hours from 06:00 to 07:00 AM in outdoor or well-ventilated setting. Focus especially on movements that support the Spleen-Stomach system (such as 'support the heavens' and 'regulate Spleen-Stomach movements'). Maintain gentle pace allowing continuous flow without vigorous intensity or rapid breathing that would deplete Qi. Purpose: Gentle flowing motion promotes healthy Qi circulation throughout meridians without the exhaustion of vigorous exercise; specific hand and body movements stimulate acupoints and meridians related to Spleen-Stomach; rhythmic breathing coordinates with movement to enhance Qi generation rather than consume it; regular practice strengthens Spleen Qi constitution over time

Gentle Walking (San Bu 散步) — Perform twenty to thirty minutes daily, timing walks to occur fifteen to twenty minutes after a light meal to support digestive function. Choose level walking paths in parks or natural settings rather than stairs or hills. Maintain pace allowing normal conversation without breathlessness. Purpose: Promotes Spleen's transport function and stimulates Qi circulation throughout the body without depleting reserves; walking after meals aids the digestive process through gentle movement; outdoor walking provides fresh air supporting Lung and Spleen coordination; consistent daily practice supports constitutional strengthening better than occasional vigorous exercise
recommendations.emotional_care: A patient with twenty years of chronic itching disorder has likely developed secondary emotional distress including frustration, despair, reduced quality of life, and social withdrawal. Recommend: (1) Cultivate acceptance and self-compassion toward the body, acknowledging that a condition taking twenty years to develop will require consistent three to six month recovery period—expecting instant results creates additional Spleen-damaging worry; (2) Implement daily stress reduction through gentle meditation (five to ten minutes) or nature walking, as anger, worry, and excessive mental activity directly damage Spleen function and perpetuate the pattern; (3) Establish regular consultation with a TCM practitioner (ideally monthly) not only for clinical assessment but for emotional support and validation, as the psychological element of chronic disease management is substantial; (4) Keep a simple food-symptom diary to identify personal triggers and build sense of agency over the condition; (5) Avoid comparison with others' healing timelines or loss of hope from internet searches, as these mental patterns inhibit Spleen function. The Spleen in TCM is associated with the capacity for transformation and positive thoughts; nurturing these psychological aspects directly supports physiological healing.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Er Miao San (Two Marvelous Powder) — Acute Phase Formula
ingredients: Chi Shao (Red Peony, Paeonia lactiflora, blood-invigorating preparation) — 12g
herbal_formulas.dosage: One 7-sachet packet decocted daily (or equivalent raw herbs decocted for 40 minutes in 600ml water, divided into two 300ml doses taken morning and evening with warm water), for seven to fourteen days during acute flare phase; after acute symptoms subside (reduced rash redness, decreased weeping, improved sleep), transition to Formula 2
herbal_formulas.purpose: This formula addresses the acute Damp-Heat manifestation while protecting Spleen Qi from iatrogenic damage. Cang Zhu and Huang Bai are bitter cold herbs that powerfully dry Dampness and clear Heat from the Lower Burner and intestines. However, these alone would damage Spleen Yang and worsen the underlying deficiency. The formula balances this with Bai Zhu and Fu Ling which fortify Spleen Qi and transformation, preventing the collateral damage from aggressive clearing. Chi Shao invigorates blood circulation in the skin layer, reducing redness and inflammatory response. Gan Cao harmonizes all ingredients and supports Spleen Qi. This combination allows clearing of acute pathogenic Damp-Heat without worsening the constitutional weakness, making it suitable for a patient with mixed Excess-Deficiency pattern.

herbal_formulas.name: Modified Si Jun Zi Tang (Four Gentlemen Decoction) — Maintenance Phase Formula
ingredients: Ren Shen (Ginseng, Panax ginseng) — 9g [or Dang Shen (Codonopsis pilosula) 15g if cost is concern]
Zhi Gan Cao (Honey-fried Licorice, Glycyrrhiza uralensis prepared) — 6g
Yi Yi Ren (Job's Tears / Coix lacryma-jobi) — 15g [added to base formula]
Hong Zao (Red Date / Jujube, Ziziphus jujuba) — 3-5 pieces [added to base formula]
herbal_formulas.dosage: One 7-sachet packet decocted daily (or raw herbs decocted for 45 minutes in 700ml water, divided into morning and evening 350ml doses), consumed warm after meals with slight honey sweetening if desired, for six to eight weeks following the acute flare resolution; may continue at reduced frequency (three to four times weekly) for additional four to eight weeks as constitutional support
herbal_formulas.purpose: Si Jun Zi Tang is the classical foundational formula for Spleen Qi supplementation, used for two thousand years in Chinese medicine for Qi deficiency with poor digestion and fatigue. The four 'gentlemen' herbs are Ren Shen (powerful Qi supplementation), Bai Zhu (strengthens Spleen's transformation), Fu Ling (drains residual Dampness while supporting Spleen), and Zhi Gan Cao (harmonization and additional Qi support). This base formula is modified by adding Job's Tears and red dates: Job's Tears provides gentle ongoing Dampness elimination while supporting the digestive transformation, and red dates supplement blood and nourish the skin, essential after twenty years of chronic skin inflammation. This formula systematically rebuilds Spleen Qi constitution, gradually increasing appetite, reducing fatigue, improving stool formation, and providing the Qi foundation necessary for skin healing. The transition from acute clearing formula to this maintenance formula is critical—attempting to sustain aggressive clearing would eventually exhaust the patient; instead, feeding the root allows the body to naturally prevent pathogenic re-accumulation.

warning_signs: Severe progression of rash with purulent (pus-filled) drainage, increasing warmth, or spreading borders within 24-48 hours—suggests possible bacterial superinfection requiring dermatology evaluation and possible topical or systemic antibiotics
Development of fever (temperature >38.5°C), chills, or enlarged lymph nodes—suggests systemic infection or inflammatory response requiring immediate medical evaluation
Worsening joint pain, swelling, or morning stiffness—could indicate systemic inflammatory or autoimmune condition requiring rheumatology evaluation
Acute worsening of fatigue, dizziness, or shortness of breath disproportionate to current skin flare—suggests possible anemia or cardiac involvement requiring hematology and cardiology assessment

Severe sleep deprivation (unable to sleep more than 2-3 hours nightly for more than one week despite interventions)—indicates need for sleep specialist evaluation and possible temporary pharmaceutical sleep support
contraindications: Absolutely avoid high-dose cooling bitter herbs such as Huang Lian (Coptis), Huang Qin (Scutellaria), Da Huang (Rheum), or Shi Gao (Gypsum) used alone or in prolonged courses—these create severe iatrogenic Spleen Yang injury, worsening the constitutional deficiency and ultimately perpetuating the skin condition

Avoid greasy tonics or excessive supplementation with warm Qi tonics (high-dose ginseng, red ginseng) without balanced cooling and Damp-clearing support—these exacerbate Damp-Heat manifestation and can trigger acute flaring

Avoid vigorous massage or gua sha (scraping) directly on inflamed skin areas during acute flare—mechanical irritation increases rash severity; gentle acupoint massage away from the most inflamed areas is acceptable

Avoid prolonged heat application (hot water baths, heating pads) to inflamed areas—while warmth supports Spleen function in general, direct heat on acute rash exacerbates the Heat component and increases itching
Avoid exposure to known personal triggers (identified through food-symptom diary) such as specific foods or environmental factors that have previously caused flaring
precautions.special_notes: This patient's twenty-year history indicates a deeply constitutional weakness that will not resolve quickly despite correct treatment. Realistic expectations are critical for compliance: expect visible improvement in three to four weeks (reduced rash severity, better sleep, improved appetite), but complete healing likely requires three to six months of consistent treatment including herbal therapy, dietary modification, and lifestyle changes. Relapses may occur if the patient returns to previous dietary habits or emotional patterns—each relapse is an opportunity to identify and address triggers rather than a treatment failure. Monthly or bi-monthly clinical reassessment is strongly recommended to adjust formulas as the patient's constitution strengthens. The transition from acute formula to maintenance formula should occur when acute inflammatory signs (redness, weeping) decrease by at least 50%, typically after one to two weeks—continuing aggressive clearing too long risks exhausting Spleen Qi and stalling recovery. If at any point fatigue worsens despite Qi-supplementing herbs, consider evaluation for underlying anemia or nutritional deficiency.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess clinical status and adjust treatment plan after two weeks of acute phase formula; if adequate improvement noted (rash redness and weeping reduced by 50%, sleep improved, appetite improving), transition to maintenance phase formula and continue for six to eight weeks with follow-up assessment at four weeks and eight weeks
follow_up.expected_improvement: Within one week of starting acute formula: reduction in itching intensity (allowing more sleep), less exudate and crusting on skin, slight mood improvement from better sleep. Within two to three weeks: visible fading of rash erythema (redness), appetite beginning to improve, energy increasing, loose stools becoming more formed. Within four to six weeks: substantial rash improvement with minimal itching, normal appetite and digestion, fatigue markedly reduced, sleep without disturbance from itching. By eight to twelve weeks: rash largely resolved with possible residual mild discoloration, normal energy levels, normal appetite and stool, restoration of quality of life; further improvement continues more slowly over three to six months as constitutional Spleen Qi fully rebuilds
follow_up.next_steps: After two-week acute phase: transition from acute Er Miao San to maintenance Si Jun Zi Tang formula and continue for six to eight weeks minimum. Concurrently, implement all dietary and lifestyle recommendations with particular emphasis on food therapy, consistent meal timing, and gentle exercise. At four-week point: assess whether additional acupoint self-massage or professional acupuncture would be beneficial (professional acupuncture once monthly would significantly enhance results). If inadequate improvement by three to four weeks despite formula compliance, consider: (1) dermatology referral to exclude fungal infection or other conditions requiring topical treatment; (2) blood work to evaluate for nutritional deficiencies (B12, iron, zinc) or endocrine dysfunction (thyroid function); (3) possible adjustment of herbal formula based on reassessment of pattern. If improvement plateaus after eight weeks, extend maintenance phase for additional four weeks, then consider transitioning to a minimal-intervention constitutional support approach (formulas three times weekly instead of daily, continued dietary therapy).

Before beginning any herbal formula, dietary changes, or new health regimen, the patient should consult with both a licensed TCM practitioner and their primary care physician to ensure compatibility with any existing medical conditions and medications. Herbal preparations may have drug interactions or contraindications. Any worsening of symptoms, emergence of new symptoms, or persistent lack of improvement after two to three weeks should prompt immediate evaluation by a qualified healthcare provider. data.wen_inquiry: Chief complaint: Twenty years of recurrent scaly red rash over the whole body with severe itching, worse in the last week. Symptoms: sticky feeling in the mouth; poor appetite; fatigue; heavy body sensation; sticky stools with incomplete evacuation; yellowish exudate and crusting on skin; itching disturbing sleep.
